title: Adverbs and Degree
summary: How an adverb is made out of an adjective, what kinds of adverb there are, and how both adjective and adverb are compared — better, best; more cheaply, most cheaply.

rules.heading: Adverbs in -ai and -iai
rules.statement: An adverb of manner is made from the **masculine** form of a qualitative adjective by changing **-as** to **-ai** and **-us** to **-iai**. It then never changes again: an adverb has no gender, no number and no case, because it belongs to the verb and not to any noun.

paradigms.caption: Adjective → adverb
paradigms.footnote: Compare ¶17: an **adjective** agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, and so has dozens of forms; an **adverb** made from the same word has exactly one.

rules.heading: Adverbs in -iškai
rules.statement: A separate suffix, **-iškai**, makes adverbs of *manner after the fashion of* — and above all the names of languages. **Kalbėti lietuviškai** is to speak Lithuanian, and the construction is an adverb throughout: the language is never a noun and never takes a case.

examples.gloss: He lives in a country fashion.

footnotes: The noun *lietuvių kalba* exists and is used of the language as a subject of study: *mokausi lietuvių kalbos*. But *kalbėti* takes the adverb.

rules.heading: The Comparative of the Adjective
rules.statement: The comparative — *aukštesnysis laipsnis* — is made with **-esnis** for the masculine and **-esnė** for the feminine, added to the stem. It then declines and agrees like any other adjective (¶17), because it is one.

paradigms.caption: Positive → comparative
paradigms.footnote: Lithuanian has no equivalent of the English choice between *-er* and *more*: every adjective forms its comparative the same way, however long it is.

examples.note: the comparative takes the accusative like any adjective

rules.heading: The Superlative of the Adjective
rules.statement: The superlative — *aukščiausiasis laipsnis* — is made with **-iausias, -iausia**. The ending begins with a back vowel, so a preceding **t** softens to *č* and **d** to *dž*, exactly as in the genitive and the past (¶28, ¶90): *greitas* gives *greičiausias*, *didelis* gives *didžiausias*.

paradigms.caption: The three degrees
paradigms.footnote: *geriausias* is built on a different stem from *geras*, as *best* is from *good*; it is the one irregularity worth noticing, and it is the commonest word of the three.

examples.gloss: Vilnius is the biggest city in Lithuania.

rules.heading: Comparing the Adverb
rules.statement: An adverb is compared with **-iau** and **-iausiai**, and undergoes the same softening before them. Because the adverb never agrees with anything, its comparative and superlative have one form each — which makes the adverb far easier to compare than the adjective.

paradigms.caption: The three degrees of the adverb
paradigms.footnote: *arti → arčiau* and *greitai → greičiau* show the softening of **t** before the back vowel of the ending, as in ¶117.

rules.heading: Than: Negu and Už
rules.statement: What is compared with is introduced by **negu** — *than* — with the second term in the **same case** as the first, since the two are being weighed against each other. Beside it stands **už** with the **accusative**, which does the same work more briefly: *didesnis už mane*, bigger than I.

paradigms.caption: The two constructions

rows.label: negu
cells: It is better here than there.

paradigms.footnote: *Už* with the genitive means *behind* (¶62) and with the accusative *for* or *than*; the case decides, as with *po* (¶75).

examples.gloss: The train is faster than the bus.
This book is more interesting than that one.

rules.heading: The Kinds of Adverb
rules.statement: Not every adverb is made from an adjective; most of the commonest are words in their own right, and they fall into five groups. Those of **quantity** deserve particular note: *daug*, *mažai*, *truputį* and *šiek tiek* all govern the **genitive** (¶32), as a numeral does.

paradigms.caption: The five groups

rows.label: place
cells: arti, toli, dešinėje, kairėje, namie, kur, čia, ten

rows.label: time
cells: dabar, rytoj, vakar, šiandien, seniai, pernai, tuoj, greitai

rows.label: quantity
cells: daug, mažai, šiek tiek, truputį, kiek, tiek

paradigms.footnote: The direction adverbs in **-n** — *kairėn*, to the left — are the remains of an old case, and are the shortest way of giving a direction: *Eikite tiesiai, paskui kairėn.*

examples.note: genitive after an adverb of quantity

examples.gloss: Go straight on, then to the right.

examples.target: Jis gyvena toli, o dirba arti.
examples.gloss: He lives far away but works near by.

vocabulary.gloss: English (in the manner of), in English

drills.explanation: An adjective in **-us** makes its adverb in **-iai**: *gražiai*. Only adjectives in *-as* give *-ai*.
A language after *kalbėti* is an **adverb** in *-iškai*, not a noun: *lietuviškai*. It therefore never takes a case.
The comparative of an adjective is **-esnis**: *mažesnis*. *mažiausias* is the superlative, and *mažai / mažiau* are adverbs.

drills.stem: Why is the superlative of **greitas** *greičiausias* and not *greitiausias*?
options: Because the ending begins with a back vowel, before which t softens to č.
Because superlatives never keep the stem consonant.
drills.explanation: The same softening met in the genitive (*savaitė → savaičių*) and in the past (*skaitė → skaičiau*). It is a rule of sound, not a peculiarity of this word.
The comparative of an adverb is **-iau**, with the t softening: *lėčiau*. *lėtai* would be merely *slowly*, and *lėčiausiai* *most slowly of all*.
After **negu** the second term matches the case of the first, so the nominative *aš*. After **už** it stands in the accusative, so *mane*. The third and fourth mix the two constructions.
An adverb of quantity governs the genitive, exactly as a word of measure does (¶32): *mažai laiko*.

options: An adverb has no gender, number or case.
Lithuanian chooses between *-esnis* and a word meaning *more*, as English chooses between *-er* and *more*.
*geriausias* is built on a different stem from *geras*.
The comparative of an adjective still agrees with its noun.
drills.explanation: There is no choice of construction: every Lithuanian adjective, however long, forms its comparative in *-esnis*. The comparative remains an adjective and goes on agreeing.

drills.stem: **Vilnius yra didžiausias Lietuvos miestas.** Why is *Lietuvos* genitive?
options: Because Lithuanian says *Lithuania's biggest city* where English says *the biggest city in Lithuania*.
drills.explanation: The genitive of possession (¶29) does the work of the English *in*. The superlative governs nothing; it is an ordinary adjective agreeing with *miestas*.

drills.stem: Into how many groups does ¶120 divide the adverbs?
drills.explanation: Five: place, direction, time, manner and quantity. Only the fourth is regularly made from adjectives; the rest are words in their own right, and those of quantity govern the genitive as numerals do.

drills.title: Kuris butas geresnis?
drills.passage: Rūta ieško buto. Pirmas butas yra centre. Jis didesnis ir gražesnis, bet daug brangesnis. Antras butas mažesnis ir pigesnis, o iki darbo eiti tik dešimt minučių — jis arčiau negu pirmas. „Manau, kad antras geriau“, — sako Rūta. „Turiu mažai pinigų, todėl brangiausio buto nepirksiu.“ Draugė sako: „Eik greičiau, kitaip jį nupirks kitas žmogus.“
drills.translation: Rūta is looking for a flat. The first flat is in the centre. It is bigger and more beautiful, but much more expensive. The second flat is smaller and cheaper, and it is only ten minutes' walk to work — it is nearer than the first. "I think the second is better," says Rūta. "I have little money, so I shall not buy the most expensive flat." Her friend says: "Go quicker, or somebody else will buy it."

questions.explanation: *Antras butas mažesnis ir pigesnis.* The comparatives agree with *butas* in the masculine nominative, as ordinary adjectives do.

questions.stem: Which words in the passage are **adverbs** in the comparative or superlative degree?
questions.explanation: *geriau*, *greičiau* and *arčiau* end in **-iau** and never change; *brangesnis* ends in *-esnis* and is an adjective, agreeing with its noun.

questions.stem: How many minutes does it take Rūta to walk to work from the second flat?
questions.explanation: *tik dešimt minučių* — ten. *dešimt* fixes the noun in the genitive plural (¶80), and *t* softens to *č* before the ending, as it does before every back vowel in the language.
